title: Reading as a Writer
description: Reading published fiction, poetry, and nonfiction the way writers do: noticing technique, asking how effects are made, and imitating models to expand your own range.
outcomes: Read published works as a writer, asking how effects are made.
Analyze and imitate sentence structures to expand stylistic range.
Study openings, scenes, dialogue, and structure in published fiction and nonfiction.
Read poems as a poet and write imitations that borrow technique.
Analyze the movement of essays and imitate their forms.
Transform influences and write in conversation with literary tradition.

weeks.title: Reading Like a Writer
weeks.overview: How writers read differently: slowing down, asking how effects are made, and keeping a craft journal.
objectives: Explain how reading as a writer differs from reading for pleasure or for interpretation.
Ask craft questions of a text.
Keep a craft journal that records techniques worth stealing.
weeks.lesson:
## Three ways of reading

You can read a story for **pleasure**, losing yourself in it. You can read it as a **critic**, asking what it means. And you can read it as a **writer**, asking *how it was made*. The writer's question is practical: what choices produced this effect, and could I use them?

Francine Prose, in *Reading Like a Writer* (2006), argues that most writers learned their craft not from classes but from close reading of books they loved, "word by word, sentence by sentence," noticing each choice. The great writers are the best teachers, and their books are always available.

## Slow down

Writers read slowly, often twice: once for the experience, then again to see how the experience was produced. On the second reading, mark:

- Places where you felt something strongly: surprise, laughter, dread, sadness.
- Sentences you admire.
- Places where you were confused or bored.

Then ask, at each mark: *What exactly is happening on the page?*

## Craft questions

Questions writers ask of a text:

- **Point of view:** Who tells this? From how close? Why this choice?
- **Opening:** How does the first paragraph orient me and make me want more?
- **Scene and summary:** Where does the writer slow down? Speed up?
- **Detail:** Which details are significant? What's left out?
- **Dialogue:** How much is said directly? What's in the subtext?
- **Structure:** How is the piece ordered? Where are the breaks?
- **Sentences:** How long are they? How do they vary? What are the verbs?
- **Ending:** What is the final image or line? How does it echo earlier moments?

## The craft journal

A **craft journal** records techniques, not opinions. Instead of "I loved this story," write: "She cuts away from the argument right at its peak and resumes the next morning, so I imagined the worst. Try in my own story." Over time, the journal becomes a personal handbook.

## Techniques worth stealing

Writers have always learned by borrowing. A line often attributed to T. S. Eliot, from his 1920 essay on Philip Massinger, says: "Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal." What he meant was that good writers absorb what they take and make it their own. Borrowing a technique, a structure, a rhythm, a way of handling time, is how craft is learned. Copying someone's words and presenting them as your own is plagiarism. This course is about the first.

### Worked example: a craft note

Reading the opening of Charles Dickens's *A Tale of Two Cities* (1859):

> It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness...

*Craft note:* "A long series of paired opposites in parallel structure, each beginning 'it was.' The repetition builds a rhythm like a drumbeat, and the contradictions announce the novel's theme of division (two cities, doubles, revolution) before any character appears. Technique: open with a pattern of contrasts that states the book's central tension."

## Common misconceptions

- **"Reading as a writer ruins the pleasure."** It usually deepens it.
- **"Imitation stifles originality."** Originality grows from absorbing many influences.
- **"Only contemporary books are useful models."** Writers learn from every era.

## Summary

Writers read to learn how effects are made. Read slowly and twice, mark moments of strong response, and ask craft questions about point of view, detail, scene, structure, sentences, and endings. Keep a craft journal of techniques, and borrow techniques, never words.

keyTerms.definition: Reading to understand how a text's effects are produced.
The techniques and choices that make up a piece of writing.
A record of techniques observed in reading, for use in one's own writing.
Repeating a grammatical pattern across phrases or sentences.
Presenting someone else's words or ideas as one's own.

weeks.title: The Sentence
weeks.overview: Studying sentences as writers: length and rhythm, syntax and emphasis, strong verbs, and the craft of imitating sentence patterns.
objectives: Analyze how sentence length, structure, and rhythm create effects.
Identify cumulative, periodic, and balanced sentences.
Imitate the structure of model sentences with new content.
weeks.lesson:
## The unit of prose

The **sentence** is the basic unit of prose style. Writers study sentences the way musicians study phrases. Virginia Tufte's *Artful Sentences* and Stanley Fish's *How to Write a Sentence* both argue that learning to write begins with learning to love sentences.

## Length and rhythm

Varying sentence length creates rhythm. A series of long sentences, followed by a short one, gives the short sentence enormous force. Gary Provost's often-quoted demonstration makes the point: write five sentences of the same length and the prose drones; vary them, and it sings.

Short sentences can create **tension**, **finality**, or **emphasis**. Long sentences can create **flow**, **accumulation**, **breathlessness**, or **complexity of thought**.

## Kinds of sentences

- **Cumulative (loose) sentence:** a main clause followed by modifiers that add detail. "She walked out into the yard, barefoot, the grass still wet, the dog trailing behind her with a stick." These feel natural and expansive.
- **Periodic sentence:** the main point is delayed until the end, creating suspense. "Through the rain, past the empty houses, over the bridge where her brother had drowned, she ran."
- **Balanced sentence:** two parts of similar structure, often in contrast. "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country."

## Emphasis

The most emphatic position in a sentence is usually the **end**; the second most emphatic is the **beginning**. Put the words that matter most where they'll be felt. Compare:

- "There was blood on the floor, I noticed when I came in."
- "When I came in, I noticed the floor. Blood."

## Verbs

Strong verbs do more work than adverbs and adjectives. "She walked slowly and heavily" is weaker than "She trudged." Vague verbs (*is*, *has*, *got*, *went*) are not wrong, but heavy reliance on them flattens prose. Look for verbs that make readers see.

## Sentence imitation

An ancient method, used in Greek and Roman rhetorical schools and by writers since, is **imitation**: copying a model sentence's *structure* exactly, while supplying entirely new content. Benjamin Franklin describes in his *Autobiography* teaching himself to write by taking notes on essays from *The Spectator*, setting them aside, and rewriting them, then comparing his versions with the originals.

### Worked example: imitating Hemingway

Ernest Hemingway's *A Farewell to Arms* (1929) begins:

> In the late summer of that year we lived in a house in a village that looked across the river and the plain to the mountains.

*Structure:* a time phrase; a simple subject and verb ("we lived"); then a chain of prepositional phrases, each moving the eye farther out, house, village, river, plain, mountains.

*Imitation:* "In the early spring of that year we rented a room above a bakery that looked over the square and the harbor to the islands."

The imitation teaches how a plain sentence can create a sweeping view by moving the reader's gaze outward step by step.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Short sentences are always better."** Variety, not brevity, creates good rhythm.
- **"Long sentences are hard to read."** Well-constructed long sentences are easy to follow.
- **"Imitation is cheating."** Structural imitation with new content is a classic training method.

## Summary

The sentence is the unit of prose style. Vary length for rhythm; use cumulative, periodic, and balanced structures for different effects; place key words at the end; prefer strong verbs; and imitate model sentence structures with new content to expand your range.

weeks.title: Studying Openings
weeks.overview: How published writers begin: first sentences, establishing voice and situation, raising questions, and when to deliver exposition.
objectives: Analyze how openings establish voice, situation, and questions.
Compare strategies for delivering exposition.
Revise an opening using techniques from models.
weeks.lesson:
## The contract

An opening makes a **contract** with readers. It establishes voice, genre, and the kind of experience to come, and it raises questions readers want answered. Readers decide in a few sentences whether to keep reading, so writers study openings closely.

## Famous first sentences

> Call me Ishmael.

Herman Melville's *Moby-Dick* (1851) opens with three words: an informal, intimate address, and a name that is a biblical outcast's. The voice is confident and conversational, inviting us into a story told by a wanderer.

> Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.

Leo Tolstoy's *Anna Karenina* (1878, in a common translation) opens with a generalization, announcing a novel about families and unhappiness.

> It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

Jane Austen's *Pride and Prejudice* (1813) states a "truth" ironically, since the novel shows that it's the families of single women who want such men. The sentence establishes Austen's ironic narrator at once.

## Strategies for openings

- **Voice first:** a distinctive narrator speaks (Melville, Twain).
- **Situation first:** we're placed in a dramatic circumstance (Kafka's transformed salesman).
- **Generalization:** a statement the story will test (Tolstoy, Austen).
- **Image or setting:** a place that establishes mood (Dickens's fog at the start of *Bleak House*).
- **Dialogue:** readers overhear a conversation already in progress.

## Questions

Strong openings raise **questions**: Who is this? What happened? What will they do? Why is this strange? Questions pull readers forward. Answer some, and raise new ones, so the momentum continues.

## Exposition

**Exposition** is background information. Beginning writers often front-load it: paragraphs of history before the story starts. Published writers usually:

- **Start with a scene** and deliver exposition in small doses.
- **Embed** background in action and dialogue.
- **Delay** exposition until readers care enough to want it.

### Worked example: comparing openings

Kate Chopin's "The Story of an Hour" (1894) opens:

> Knowing that Mrs. Mallard was afflicted with a heart trouble, great care was taken to break to her as gently as possible the news of her husband's death.

In one sentence, Chopin establishes the protagonist, a physical vulnerability (her heart), the central event (her husband's death), and the careful, gentle social world around her. The heart trouble is a planted detail that will matter at the end. And there is a question, how will she react?, which the story answers in an unexpected way.

*Craft lesson:* a single sentence can deliver character, situation, and a planted detail while raising a question. No front-loaded exposition is needed.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Openings need action."** They need tension or interest, which can come from voice or situation.
- **"Readers need all the background first."** Readers tolerate, and enjoy, not knowing everything.
- **"The first sentence must be dazzling."** It must invite; brilliance is optional.

## Summary

Openings establish voice, situation, and questions. Writers open with voice, situation, generalization, image, or dialogue, and they deliver exposition gradually, embedded in scene. Study openings to learn how much a single sentence can do.

A question raised by a story that pulls readers forward.

weeks.title: Studying Scenes and Dialogue
weeks.overview: Taking published scenes apart: pacing, beats, dialogue and subtext, and how writers move between scene and summary.
objectives: Break a published scene into its beats.
Analyze dialogue for subtext and characterization.
Identify how writers transition between scene and summary.
weeks.lesson:
## Taking a scene apart

A **scene** is built of **beats**: small units of action, reaction, or change. Reading as a writer, you can map a scene beat by beat to see how it moves: what each character wants, how the balance of power shifts, and where the turn comes.

## The beat map

For each beat, note:

1. **What happens** (an action, line, or perception).
2. **What it does** (raises tension, reveals character, shifts power, delays).
3. **Where the scene turns.**

## Dialogue as action

In good fiction, dialogue is a form of **action**: characters use words to get what they want, deflect, attack, or hide. Studying dialogue in published work, ask:

- What does each speaker **want** from this exchange?
- What do they **avoid saying**?
- How do speech patterns **characterize** them?
- How are the lines **tagged** and **punctuated** with beats?

### Worked example: "Hills Like White Elephants"

Ernest Hemingway's story (1927) is almost entirely dialogue between an American man and a young woman, Jig, waiting for a train in Spain. They never name the subject of their conversation, which most readers understand to be an abortion the man wants her to have.

The scene's power comes from **subtext**. When she says the hills look like white elephants, she is reaching for something imaginative and alive; he responds flatly. He repeatedly insists the procedure is "perfectly simple" and that he'll go along "if you want," while clearly pressing her. Near the end, she asks him to please, please, please stop talking. The repetition shows what she cannot say directly.

*Beat map (partial):*

- She remarks on the hills; he dismisses it → distance between them established.
- He raises "the operation" indirectly; she goes quiet → power shifts to him.
- She mocks his reassurances → resistance.
- She asks him to stop talking → the scene's emotional climax.

*Craft lessons:* objective point of view forces readers to read subtext; repetition reveals pressure; an image (the hills) carries the unspoken subject.

## Scene and summary

Writers move between **scene** (real-time, detailed) and **summary** (compressed time). Study how they **transition**: a white space; a time phrase ("Three weeks later"); a summary sentence that bridges into a new scene. Notice how much a published story summarizes. Beginners often dramatize everything, which slows stories; skilled writers dramatize only what matters most.

## Pacing

**Pacing** is the speed at which a story moves. Writers control it with:

- **Scene** (slow) and **summary** (fast).
- **Sentence length**: short sentences speed up action scenes.
- **White space** and section breaks.
- **Detail density**: lingering on detail slows time.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Dialogue should convey information."** In good fiction, dialogue is primarily action and characterization.
- **"Every moment should be a scene."** Summary is essential for pacing.
- **"Subtext means being vague."** Subtext is precise; it's just beneath the surface.

## Summary

Scenes are built from beats that shift power and turn. Dialogue is action: characters use words to pursue and conceal desires. Writers move between scene and summary to control pacing. Mapping published scenes reveals how these techniques work.

weeks.title: Studying Structure
weeks.overview: How published works are built: chronology and its alternatives, frames, braids, segments, and reverse outlining a model.
objectives: Reverse outline a published work to reveal its structure.
Compare chronological, framed, braided, and segmented structures.
Choose a structure that serves a piece's meaning.
weeks.lesson:
## Structure is meaning

**Structure** is the arrangement of a work's parts. The same events, arranged differently, produce different stories. Ask of any published piece: why this order?

## The reverse outline

To see a work's structure, make a **reverse outline**: list each section or scene with a short phrase describing what happens and what it does. Then look at the list:

- Where does time move forward, backward, or pause?
- Where are the big turns?
- How long is each part relative to the whole?
- What patterns or repetitions emerge?

## Common structures

### Chronological

Events in time order. The default, and often best, choice for clarity and suspense.

### Frame

A **frame** surrounds a story with another narrative. Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein* (1818) is framed by an explorer's letters to his sister; within them, Victor Frankenstein tells his story, and within *that*, the creature tells his. The nested frames let us hear multiple perspectives and question each narrator.

### Retrospective

A narrator looks back from a later point. Many first-person novels and memoirs use this, creating the double perspective of the narrating and experiencing selves.

### Braided

Two or more strands alternate and illuminate each other: a present story and a past one, or a personal story and a historical one.

### Segmented (or collage)

Short sections separated by white space, juxtaposed rather than connected by transitions. Meaning emerges between the pieces.

### Circular

The ending returns to the opening image or situation, transformed by everything between.

## Proportion

Notice how much space published writers give to each part. A story might spend a page on the inciting incident and five on a single climactic scene. **Proportion** signals importance: what writers dwell on, readers feel.

### Worked example: reverse outlining "The Story of an Hour"

Kate Chopin's very short story can be outlined:

1. Friends break the news of Brently Mallard's death to his wife, carefully, because of her heart. *(situation)*
2. She weeps, then goes alone to her room. *(expected grief)*
3. At the open window, she sees signs of spring and new life. *(images, shift begins)*
4. A feeling approaches her; she whispers "free, free, free!" *(turn)*
5. She imagines the years ahead belonging to herself. *(expansion)*
6. She descends the stairs; her husband walks in, alive. *(reversal)*
7. She dies; the doctors say of "joy that kills." *(ironic ending)*

*What the outline reveals:* the story is almost perfectly balanced around the turn at the window. The longest passages are internal, her private awakening, which is the story's real subject. The final reversal takes only a few lines. And the ending returns to the opening's heart trouble, now bitterly ironic.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Structure is only for long works."** Short pieces are often the most carefully structured.
- **"Non-chronological structures are more sophisticated."** Choose the structure that serves the piece.
- **"Structure is decided before writing."** Many writers discover structure in revision.

## Summary

Structure is meaning. Reverse outline published works to see how they're built. Writers choose among chronological, framed, retrospective, braided, segmented, and circular structures, and they use proportion to signal what matters most.

weeks.title: Reading Poems as a Poet
weeks.overview: What poets learn from other poets: lineation, image patterns, sound, and forms, studied through public-domain models and imitation.
objectives: Analyze lineation, sound, and image patterns in model poems.
Write imitations that borrow a poem's structure or technique.
Use constraint and form as tools for invention.
weeks.lesson:
## Poets read poets

Poets have always apprenticed themselves to other poets. Reading as a poet means asking not "what does it mean?" but "how is it built?"

## What to look for

- **The first line:** how does the poem enter?
- **Lineation:** where do lines break, and what words end them?
- **Stanza:** how are lines grouped?
- **Image pattern:** which images recur or develop?
- **Sound:** rhyme, alliteration, assonance, rhythm.
- **Syntax:** how do sentences move across lines?
- **The turn:** where does the poem shift?
- **The last line:** how does it close?

## Models and imitation

An **imitation** (sometimes called a model poem) borrows a poem's structure, pattern, or technique while supplying new content. Poets imitate:

- **Syntax:** follow the sentence structure line by line.
- **Pattern:** a list, a repeated phrase, a question-and-answer.
- **Form:** sonnet, villanelle, ghazal, blues.
- **Gesture:** an apostrophe, an instruction, a prayer.

### Worked example: imitating Blake's "The Tyger"

William Blake's "The Tyger" (1794) begins:

> Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
> In the forests of the night;
> What immortal hand or eye,
> Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

*Technique:* apostrophe to a creature; trochaic rhythm; a series of questions about its making that are never answered; images of fire and forging.

*Imitation (new content):*

> Spider, spider, spinning fine
> in the corner of the mine,
> what patient engine, what design
> could wind such silver from the dark?

The imitation borrows the apostrophe, rhythm, and questioning structure. Writing it teaches how questions can generate awe and how a trochaic beat creates incantation.

## Learning from Dickinson

Emily Dickinson's poems teach compression, slant rhyme, dashes, and surprising abstraction made concrete:

> Hope is the thing with feathers –
> That perches in the soul –

Imitation: choose an abstraction (grief, envy, patience), and define it as a concrete creature or object, extending the metaphor across stanzas, using dashes for pauses.

## Learning from Whitman

Walt Whitman's catalogs teach anaphora and expansive free verse lines. In "I Hear America Singing" (1860), each line names a worker and their song: the mechanic, the carpenter, the mason, the boatman. Imitation: "I hear my city..." followed by a list of specific people and sounds.

## Constraint as invention

Formal constraints, such as rhyme, meter, repetition, or a fixed number of lines, push writers toward words they wouldn't otherwise find. The **Oulipo** group of French writers, founded in 1960, made constraint a deliberate method, writing under rules such as avoiding a letter entirely. Even modest constraints, like "every line must contain a color," can unlock new poems.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Imitation produces derivative poems."** Imitation is practice; the poems you write afterward are richer for it.
- **"Free verse can't be imitated."** Its syntax, catalogs, and line lengths are imitable.
- **"Constraint limits creativity."** It often sparks it.

## Summary

Reading as a poet means studying lineation, stanzas, images, sound, syntax, and turns. Imitations borrow syntax, pattern, form, or gesture with new content. Models such as Blake, Dickinson, and Whitman teach specific techniques, and constraints can be engines of invention.

A list, often extended, used as a poetic structure.
A formal rule a writer adopts to shape writing.
A French group of writers, founded in 1960, who write under formal constraints.

weeks.title: Reading Nonfiction as a Writer
weeks.overview: How essayists work: voice in nonfiction, the essayistic mind at work, reflection, and the forms of the essay from Montaigne to the present.
objectives: Analyze voice and the movement of thought in essays.
Identify how essayists integrate scene, information, and reflection.
Imitate an essay's form or movement.
weeks.lesson:
## The mind on the page

What distinguishes an essay is the sense of a **mind at work**, a writer thinking in real time, testing ideas, changing their mind. Reading essays as a writer, watch how the thinking moves.

## Montaigne, the first essayist

Michel de Montaigne, a sixteenth-century French nobleman, retired to his tower library and began writing short pieces he called *essais*, "attempts." His subjects ranged from friendship and cannibals to thumbs and smells. His motto was "*Que sais-je?*" ("What do I know?"). Montaigne's essays wander, digress, contradict themselves, and quote classical authors, and that wandering is their point: they show a mind exploring.

## Voice in nonfiction

Essay voices range from intimate and confessional to cool and analytical. Study:

- **How the essayist addresses the reader.**
- **How much the "I" appears.**
- **Tone:** humor, anger, tenderness, irony.
- **Diction:** formal or colloquial.

### Example: Orwell's plain style

George Orwell's essay "Shooting an Elephant" (1936) opens:

> In Moulmein, in Lower Burma, I was hated by large numbers of people—the only time in my life that I have been important enough for this to happen to me.

The sentence is plain, direct, and self-deprecating, with a dry irony that will turn darker as the essay examines his role as a colonial policeman. Orwell's later essay "Politics and the English Language" (1946) argues for this very plainness: prefer short words, cut needless ones, and avoid stale metaphors.

## Moves of the essay

Essayists combine several moves:

- **Scene:** dramatized experience.
- **Information:** facts, history, research.
- **Reflection:** interpretation and meaning.
- **Turn:** a shift in thought, often signaled by "But" or "And yet."

Mapping these moves in a published essay reveals its rhythm: how much scene, how much information, where the thinking turns.

## The essayistic turn

Many great essays turn on a moment where the writer's understanding shifts. In "Shooting an Elephant," Orwell, pressed by a crowd, realizes that the colonizer, too, is trapped by the role he plays: "when the white man turns tyrant it is his own freedom that he destroys." The scene of the elephant becomes an insight about empire.

## Forms

Essays take many forms:

- **Narrative essay:** built on a story.
- **Lyric essay:** fragmentary and poetic.
- **Braided essay:** interweaving strands.
- **Hermit crab essay:** borrowing another form's "shell," such as a list, recipe, or set of instructions, a term from Brenda Miller and Suzanne Paola's *Tell It Slant*.

### Worked example: mapping moves

A paragraph-by-paragraph map of an essay on a grandfather's garden:

1. Scene: digging potatoes with him, age eight.
2. Information: the history of potato famines in his home country.
3. Scene: his hands, his silence when asked about the past.
4. Reflection: what silence protects.
5. Turn: "But I've come to think the garden was his way of talking."
6. Scene: the writer's own garden, decades later.

The map reveals a braid of scene and information, a single turn, and a circular return to the garden.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Essays must have a thesis stated at the start."** Literary essays often discover their meaning as they go.
- **"Nonfiction voice should be neutral."** Essay voices are often vivid and personal.
- **"Research and personal writing don't mix."** Many great essays braid both.

## Summary

Essays show a mind at work, a tradition begun by Montaigne. Study voice, the moves of scene, information, reflection, and turn, and forms from narrative to lyric, braided, and hermit crab essays. Map an essay's moves to see how its thinking unfolds.

weeks.title: Influence and Originality
weeks.overview: Making influences your own: tradition and the individual writer, the reading life, building a personal canon, and writing in conversation with other works.
objectives: Explain how writers transform their influences.
Build a personal canon of model texts.
Write a piece in conversation with a published work.
weeks.lesson:
## The anxiety of influence

Every writer is influenced. The critic Harold Bloom called this the "anxiety of influence": the struggle of writers to find their own voice against the power of their predecessors. T. S. Eliot took a different view in "Tradition and the Individual Talent" (1919): writers become individual by deeply absorbing tradition, not by avoiding it. "No poet, no artist of any art, has his complete meaning alone."

## How writers transform influence

Writers make influences their own by:

- **Combining** several influences, so no single one dominates.
- **Changing context:** applying a technique to a new subject.
- **Responding:** answering, arguing with, or revising an earlier work.
- **Exaggerating** or **subverting** a technique.

## Writing in conversation

Literature is a long conversation. Writers respond to earlier works through:

- **Retellings:** a familiar story from a new perspective. Jean Rhys's *Wide Sargasso Sea* (1966) imagines the life of the "madwoman in the attic" from *Jane Eyre*.
- **Answer poems:** Sir Walter Raleigh's "The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd" (1600) answers Christopher Marlowe's "The Passionate Shepherd to His Love," turning a seductive invitation into a skeptical refusal.
- **Allusion:** brief references that bring another work into play.
- **Homage:** borrowing a form or opening as a tribute.

### Worked example: an answer poem

Marlowe's shepherd invites:

> Come live with me and be my love,
> And we will all the pleasures prove,

Raleigh's nymph replies:

> If all the world and love were young,
> And truth in every shepherd's tongue,
> These pretty pleasures might me move
> To live with thee and be thy love.

Raleigh keeps Marlowe's meter, rhyme, and phrases but turns them inside out: the nymph points out that flowers fade, winter comes, and shepherds lie. The answer poem teaches that responding to a work can create something new and pointed.

## Building a personal canon

A **personal canon** is the set of works a writer returns to for instruction and inspiration. Build yours deliberately:

- **Range widely:** across centuries, cultures, and genres.
- **Read in translation.**
- **Include contemporary writers** alongside classics.
- **Return:** reread favorite works at different stages of your writing life.
- **Note why:** for each work, record what it teaches you.

## The reading life

Writers read constantly. Ursula K. Le Guin, Toni Morrison, and many others described reading as the foundation of writing. A practical habit: read for at least as long as you write each week, and read at least some work outside your comfort zone.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Original writers avoid influence."** Originality comes from transforming influences.
- **"Retellings are unoriginal."** Many celebrated works are retellings.
- **"Only classics belong in a canon."** A personal canon includes anything that teaches you.

## Course synthesis

You've learned to read as a writer: to study sentences, openings, scenes, structure, poems, and essays; to imitate models; and to write in conversation with tradition. These habits of attention will continue to teach you for as long as you read.

## Summary

All writers are influenced; they become original by combining, recontextualizing, responding to, and transforming their influences. Literature is a conversation of retellings, answers, allusions, and homages. Build a personal canon deliberately and keep a lifelong reading practice.
